items.e: **Laws of slaughter on Yom Tov. Contains 20 sections** One may not show a knife to a scholar on Yom Tov to determine whether it is fit for slaughter, lest it be found notched and he tell him it is forbidden to slaughter with it, and he will go and sharpen it on a whetstone. A scholar who examined a knife for himself may lend it to others. Rema: Nowadays since every slaughterer examines his own knife, anyone wishing to slaughter on Yom Tov should examine his knife before Yom Tov and not on Yom Tov lest he sharpen it. However if he did not examine it before Yom Tov and it is a pressing situation, he may examine it on Yom Tov.

One may bring a knife and an animal to a butcher to slaughter, even a small kid that must be carried on one's shoulder, even though it was possible to bring it yesterday. (And similarly the butcher may bring the knife to the animal.)

Animals that go out and graze beyond the boundary and come and sleep within the boundary are considered prepared, and one may take them and slaughter them on Yom Tov. But animals that graze and sleep beyond the boundary — if they came on Yom Tov, one may not slaughter them on Yom Tov since they are set-aside and the townspeople had no intention regarding them. This applies to animals belonging to Jews, but those belonging to non-Jews have no set-aside concern since non-Jews require no preparation — unless they were brought for the sake of a Jew, in which case it is forbidden. Therefore if a non-Jew brought animals to the slaughterhouse and it is known they slept beyond the boundary, they are forbidden; if there is doubt, they are permitted even if they were brought for a Jew, since set-aside is treated leniently in cases of doubt. If they were brought for the non-Jew or even without specification in a city with a non-Jewish majority, it is permitted since whoever brings for the majority brings for all.

Animals known to sleep beyond the boundary that are found in the city on the second day — I say perhaps they were brought in the evening before, and those that slept outside the walls are permitted. All the more so animals slaughtered in the morning, where there is a presumption they were brought within the boundary the previous evening.

A calf born on Yom Tov may be slaughtered if its mother is designated for eating and it is known with certainty that its months of gestation were completed. Rema: It is also required that it have stood on the ground, since we are concerned lest an internal organ defect be found and it turn out the slaughter on Yom Tov was unnecessary — so it appears to me from the words of the Rosh and the Tur. If Shabbat and Yom Tov are adjacent, one born on one may be slaughtered on the other.

A dangerously ill animal that one fears may die — if one has already eaten and does not need it — it is forbidden to slaughter it unless there is enough time in the day to eat an olive's worth of roasted meat while it is still day (even if there is not enough time to cut it up and examine it first) . When there is enough time and one slaughtered it, one may not remove its hide unless one left one limb attached and brings it along. Rema: Some say it should not be skinned at all unless it was slaughtered for Yom Tov purposes, and this is the proper ruling.
If one slaughtered an animal in the field, he may not bring it on a pole or carrying frame as one does on a weekday, but must bring it by hand limb by limb.

A bird that was trampled underfoot where there is concern that its organs were crushed — and therefore requires waiting a full day and examination after slaughter — may be slaughtered on Yom Tov, and we are not concerned that it may be found to be a trefah, even though a defect has arisen in it.

A firstborn animal in our time that cannot be slaughtered without a blemish — a scholar may not examine it on Yom Tov to determine whether it has a blemish. Even if he transgressed and examined it and found a blemish, he may not slaughter it. But if it was born with its blemish and he transgressed and examined it, it may be slaughtered on his ruling. If he examined the blemish before Yom Tov and saw it was a blemish warranting slaughter, he may investigate on Yom Tov whether the blemish arose on its own and thereby permit it. Rema: If a firstborn fell into a pit, it is forbidden to lift it out since it cannot be slaughtered — rather one provides for it in its place.

If a mother animal and her offspring both fell into a pit, one lifts out the first intending to slaughter it but does not slaughter it, then cunningly lifts out the second — whichever one he wishes he may slaughter.
An animal half owned by a non-Jew and half by a Jew may be slaughtered on Yom Tov, and even if they have two such animals both may be slaughtered.
One who slaughters an animal on Yom Tov may not pull out the wool to make room for the knife, but moves it aside (by hand) and draws it this way and that — and if it comes out, it comes out.
One who slaughters a bird may not pluck the feathers to make room for the knife.

A person may not slaughter a wild animal or bird on Yom Tov unless he has earth prepared before Yom Tov. If he transgressed and slaughtered, if he has a pointed implement (meaning a type of iron spike with which one digs the ground) stuck in loose earth from before Yom Tov, he may cover the blood with it. (Even if several pokings were required, it is permitted.)

Ashes from a stove that was heated before Yom Tov may be used for covering. But if it was heated on Yom Tov, it is forbidden unless the ashes are hot enough to roast an egg. If one slaughtered, one may cover with them even if they are not hot enough to roast an egg. Nevertheless it is preferable to cover with a pointed implement in loose earth if available.

If one brought a large quantity of earth into his house for his garden and it is piled in one place, one may cover with it — since as long as it is piled up he has it in mind for whatever he needs. But if he brought in only a basketful for his garden, it is voided since it is so little.

One may bring a full basket of earth into his house without specification and use it for all his needs (see above Siman 308, section 38) — and we do not say it is voided relative to the ground of the house — provided he designated a corner for it, since as long as he did not spread it out it is evident he needs it for his purposes. And if it is loose earth, one may cover with it.

A koy (meaning a creature born from a goat and a deer) — one may not slaughter it on Yom Tov, and if one did slaughter it, one may not cover its blood even with prepared earth, since an observer will say it is certainly a wild animal — otherwise why would they trouble to cover its blood on Yom Tov — and he will come to permit its forbidden fat. If its mark is recognizable, one may cover it. Rema: This applies specifically when it was slaughtered in a corner and similar situations. But if it was slaughtered in the middle of the courtyard, even the blood of a regular animal may be covered if one has prepared earth, since it is like an offensive object that must be covered so that one's clothes not be soiled in the courtyard.

If one slaughtered an animal and a wild animal and their blood became mixed, and one has prepared earth or stove ashes — if one can cover it with a single poking without needing to do more on account of the animal's blood, one may cover it; if not, one may not.
If one slaughtered a bird before Yom Tov and did not cover its blood, one may not cover it on Yom Tov.

**Laws of salting and removing feathers on Yom Tov. Containing 5 paragraphs:** One does not defeather using the margil method on Yom Tov. What is this margil method? It is when one removes all the flesh from one leg in order to remove the entire hide intact without it tearing because the effort of this skinning is a great effort, and there is no need for it on the festival.
It is forbidden to boil a kid unless you boil it to eat the skin.

Regarding an animal that was slaughtered on Yom Tov, it is permissible to remove its skin and put it in an area of foot traffic even though there is no meat on it, and it is permissible to salt it lightly like the way we salt for roasting, and it is permissible to trick (by leaving bits of meat) and salt here and there until you salt the whole thing, but if it was slaughtered before Yom Tov it is forbidden. Rama: and feathers of birds their rule is like that of skin, that you are allowed to move them to save them, like skin.
One may not salt fats on Yom Tov or flip them, or even to put then on stakes, even if it was slaughtered on Yom tov, it is also forbidden to salt meat over them in the air.

A pestle that is thick and heavy is considered a vessel, but its designated use is for a prohibited purpose—to crush herbs with it. It is permitted to move it in order to cut meat upon it. But after one has cut upon it, it is forbidden to move it from sun to shade. [However, for its own sake or for the sake of its place, it is permitted.]

One should not purchase meat with a fixed price, saying to the butcher "give me [meat worth] a sela or two." Nor should one say to him "I am a partner with you for a sela." Rather, he divides for them thirds or quarters according to the portions that are customary to divide in the city, without a fixed price. And he brings two animals and says "this one is like that one," and tomorrow they assess what remains according to its value, and that is how he pays him. Rema: And some say that specifically a Jew with regard to a Jew is permitted in this manner, but a Jew with a non-Jew, even in this manner it is forbidden. [Hagahot Ashiri, chapter Ein Tzadin]

It is prohibited to weigh meat, even in one’s home, to determine how much to cook. It is not even permitted to place meat in the cup of a scale to keep it from mice if it is suspended in the place where it is normally weighed. One may not even weigh one piece of meat against another piece of meat. It is permitted to weigh meat by hand by taking it in one’s hand and estimating its weight but a professional butcher may not even do that. If he is capable of cutting meat in the size of a litra or half-litra he may cut it in a normal manner without concerns.
It is prohibited to pierce a hole in meat so that it could be suspended but by hand is permitted. If the intent is to mark the meat it is permitted even with a knife

One may scald the head and feet [of an animal] and pass them through fire, but one may not plaster them with lime, clay, or earth, as this appears like tanning. And one may not shear them with scissors, as this appears like preparing for the sake of the hair.

It is permitted to salt several pieces [of meat] at once, even though one only needs one. Rema: And some say that this circumvention is only permitted before the morning meal. It is permitted to salt meat on a festival even though it was possible to salt it before the festival (Maharil and Terumat HaDeshen §80).

The custom is to remove forbidden fats and sinews on a festival, even if the animal was slaughtered before the festival. [And it is good to vary the procedure somewhat, if one can vary in some way] (Maharil and Terumat HaDeshen §84).

It is prohibited to chop wood from beams which are set aside for construction or from beams that broke on Yom Tov even if it was weak before Yom Tov and was about to break. If it broke before Yom Tov and cannot not be used as fuel for a fire without chopping it one may chop large pieces. One may not use an ax, sickle, or a saw; rather one should use a chopper (A butcher’s knife and some make it with two heads resembling an ax) but one should use the narrow head rather than the wide head. Some prohibit even the use of a chopper since we are not experts to identify what is a chopper and only permit the use of a knife.
Wood that is somewhat large but suitable for kindling without splitting, one should not split it at all, and even breaking it by hand, there are those who forbid.

We do not bring wood from the field, even if it was gathered there from the eve of the holiday. However, one may gather in the field from what is directly before him (and likewise in a courtyard, one takes from before him) [Beit Yosef and Rambam] and kindle there. And one may bring wood from what is gathered in a private domain, even if it was enclosed not for dwelling purposes, provided that it has a doorframe and is within the Shabbat boundary. If it lacks any one of these conditions, the wood is muktzeh.

Reed leaves and vine leaves—even though they are gathered in an enclosure, since the wind scatters them, they are considered as if scattered and are forbidden. But if one placed a heavy vessel upon them before Yom Tov, they are considered prepared.
Wood that fell from a tree on Yom Tov—one may not use it for kindling. (See further above, section 506, paragraph 2.)

Vessels that broke on Yom Tov may not be used for kindling because they are newly designated. (And if one kindled with vessels, it is forbidden to stir the fire after they have been partially ignited, for then they become broken vessel pieces, unless one has added prepared wood to them) [Maggid chapter 2 and Ran, first chapter of Beitzah]. But one may kindle with whole vessels or with vessels that broke while it was still day.

Almonds and nuts that one ate before Yom Tov—one may kindle with their shells on Yom Tov. But if one ate them on Yom Tov, one may not kindle with their shells. Gloss: Also, one should not kindle with the almonds and nuts themselves unless they are still in their shells (Beit Yosef). And torches that remained from the first Yom Tov that went out—it is permitted to relight them even on the second day of Rosh Hashanah or on Yom Tov following Shabbat [Rosh and Mordechai, beginning of Beitzah, and Beit Yosef].

**Laws of fire on Yom Tov. 4 sections:** One may not produce fire from wood, stones, earth, or water; one may not make charcoal; one may not blow with bellows but only with a tube — and the custom has been to permit using household bellows with a change by inverting it from top to bottom. Rema: It is permitted to cover a fire with a vessel or with prepared earth if one does not extinguish it, and specifically for the needs of the first day of Yom Tov — but for the needs of the second day it is forbidden. (Maharil) One who makes a bonfire on Yom Tov — when arranging the wood he does not place one piece on top of another until the arrangement is complete, since it appears like building; rather he either throws the wood in a jumbled manner or arranges it with a change. How so? He places a piece on top and then puts another beneath it and another beneath that until he reaches the ground. Similarly with a pot — he holds it and places the stones beneath it, but does not place it on top of the stones. Similarly with a bed — he holds the boards above and inserts the legs beneath them. Even eggs one should not stack row upon row like a tower, but should change and start from top to bottom. Similarly all such things require a change. Rema: Similarly a table with sides that reach the ground (Tosafot) requires a change. But it is permitted to set up our ordinary table on its legs and there is no concern of building. Some say that even if it reaches the ground, as long as one does not need the airspace beneath it, it is permitted. (Tur)

A bundle of wood that was lit in a bonfire — any piece of wood not yet caught by the fire may be pulled out, and this is not comparable to removing oil from a lamp. Rema: It is permitted to take a burning piece of wood from one side of the bonfire and place it on the other side, since one does not intend to extinguish it. (Mordechai)

One may not use a piece of split wood to prop up a pot or a door. Rema: But it is permitted to roast with it. (Rif) All the more so it is permitted to kindle with it together with other wood, even though it is not suitable for kindling on its own. (Ran)

According to our practice it is permitted to cook in new pots on Yom Tov. Rema: Some forbid it (Rosh and Tur) and this is the custom, except in a pressing situation. Therefore the custom is that when one buys new pots for Pesach one cooks in them before Yom Tov. (own opinion)

**Not to prepare on one Yom Tov for the next. 2 sections:** It is forbidden to bake, cook, or slaughter on Yom Tov for the needs of the next day — even if it is Shabbat or Yom Tov, and even for the two days of Rosh Hashanah. However, a woman may fill a pot with meat even though she only needs one piece. Rema: All the more so one may slaughter even though one only needs a small amount. (Semak) Similarly one may cook many pots and eat a little from each one. [Beit Yosef, Rabbeinu Yerucham, and responsum of Rashba] This applies specifically before eating, but after eating she may not cook and claim she will eat a little from it, as that would be a ruse. However if she transgressed and cooked [or slaughtered], it is permitted to eat it.

A baker may fill an entire barrel of water even though he only needs one jug. Rema: But he must place everything near the fire at once — it is forbidden to add more once the barrel is already near the fire, as that is unnecessary extra effort. (HaMagid ch. 1)

**Laws of spices on Yom Tov. 4 sections:** Spices may be pounded in the normal way, since if they were pounded the day before their flavor would dissipate. But salt may not be pounded on Yom Tov unless one tilts the mortar or pounds it in a bowl or similar vessel in order to make a change — since if salt were ground before Yom Tov its flavor would not dissipate. Pepper and mustard may not be ground in their special mills since that appears like a weekday activity; rather one pounds them in a mortar like all other spices. Rema: Nevertheless the custom is to make a slight change when pounding spices. (Hagahot Maimoniyot ch. 3 in the name of Semag) And this is the proper ruling.
It is permitted to carry spices and a pestle to a mortar, or a mortar to them, even through a public domain, even though it would have been possible to bring them before Yom Tov.

One may not pound groats in a large mortar, but one may pound them in a small mortar — that being the change applicable to them. In the Land of Israel even a small mortar is forbidden. Since we no longer know what is called large or small, everything should be forbidden. Rema: It is permitted to grate cheese on Yom Tov on a grater, however a slight change is required, like the pounding of salt. [Rivash §184] The same applies to matzah without any change, since there is no grinding prohibition for foods that were already ground. [Maharil]
A person is permitted to measure spices to put into a pot so that he does not ruin his dish (meaning so that he does not burn and spoil it using too many spices)

Laws of kneading on Yom Tov. Containing 9 paragraphs: One may not measure flour on Yom Tov in order to knead, but rather should take an estimated amount. Rema: And it is permitted to take flour from the container even though one makes a pit in the flour [Ran, first chapter of Beitzah and chapter Kirah].

One may not sift flour, even with a variation [from the usual method]. However, if it was sifted yesterday and a pebble or wood chip fell into it and one wishes to sift it a second time, it is permitted even without variation. Rema: And there are those who say that it is permitted to remove the pebble or wood chip by hand (Rashba). But there are those who are strict and forbid it [Maggid chapter 3]. And if nothing fell into it but one wishes to sift it a second time in order that the bread be nice, a slight variation is required, such as [sifting] on top of a table. Rema: And similarly it is permitted to do it through a non-Jew, even the initial sifting, if he varies it slightly [Beit Yosef].

One who kneaded dough on Yom Tov may separate challah from it and bring it to the kohen [it is permitted even if he separated it the day before]. But dough that was kneaded before Yom Tov—it is forbidden to separate challah from it on Yom Tov. Rema: Rather, he should eat and leave over a bit, and tomorrow separate challah from what was left over. And it is permitted to bake the bread by means of eating from it and separating challah afterwards [Beit Yosef]. And if he wishes, he can knead another dough on Yom Tov and combine them together, and separate from that dough also for what he kneaded before Yom Tov [Hagahot Maimoniot chapter 3, Mordechai chapter Elu Overin, and Beit Yosef in the name of Tosafot, first chapter of Beitzah].
One who separates challah on Yom Tov and it is impure he should not bake it nor burn it, for we do not burn sacred items on Yom Tov. Rather, he should set it aside until evening and burn it.
It is permitted to make large loaves on Yom Tov, and we are not concerned that through this one will come to bake more than what is needed.
"If one had flour or dough in partnership with a non-Jew, it is forbidden to bake it on Yom Tov; rather, he should divide it and bake his own [portion]."
If a person has much fine bread, he may not bake other bread unless he has household members whom he regularly feeds coarse bread. But if he has much coarse bread, he may bake fine bread.
It is forbidden to make leaven on Yom Tov except with an alteration, because it was possible to make it while it was still day [before Yom Tov].
Even if the animal was slaughtered on the eve of Yom Tov, it is permitted to separate the gifts on Yom Tov.

**Laws of baking on Yom Tov. Containing 7 pargraphs: ** One may bake in a forni which is our large ovens whose openings are on their side provided it is not new, for we are concerned that it might crack and the bread will be ruined and prevent the joy of Yom Tov. And one may heat water in an antiki [meaning: a large pot] .

Even though wood that fell from a palm tree on Yom Tov or on the Shabbat preceding it is forbidden to kindle, if the wood fell on Yom Tov into the oven, one may add prepared wood upon it [so that the forbidden wood should not be recognizable] (Ran, first chapter of Beitzah) and nullify it, provided that one does not touch it until it is nullified in the majority. But if the wood fell into the oven on Shabbat, it is forbidden to kindle it on the Yom Tov that follows, even through nullification in the majority.
It is forbidden to take wood from among logs to stoke the fire in an oven, for this constitutes repairing a vessel.

It is forbidden to take wood from among logs to stoke the fire in an oven, for this constitutes repairing a vessel. If an oven has plaster-clay fall into it: if it is possible to bake and roast in it without sweeping and the bread or roast will not be scorched, it is forbidden to sweep it out because one is moving it unnecessarily. But it is permitted to flatten the fire and the ash in it so that it will be smooth and will not touch the bread at all, even though if it were touching it, it would not be enough to scorch it. However, if there is enough of the plaster that fell into it to scorch the bread or roast if it were touching them, even though without sweeping it would be possible to bake and roast in it, since it scorches, it is permitted to sweep it out, for this is considered moving for a purpose. This applies specifically to their ovens, where they would attach the bread around the sides and only needed to sweep out the plaster that fell into it. But our ovens, since it is impossible to bake in them without sweeping, it is permitted to sweep it from the ash and coals, and even though one extinguishes [fire in the process], it is impossible otherwise. And just as it is permitted to kindle for the purpose of food preparation, so too it is permitted to extinguish for the purpose of food preparation. This is like placing meat on coals, and such is the custom.

A new oven and new stoves may not be coated with oil nor wiped with a cloth, but it is permitted to heat them even for the first heating, provided that one does not cool them with cold water in order to seal them. And if they were heated too much and it became necessary to cool them with cold water in order to be able to bake in them, it is permitted. Therefore, it is permitted to soak the broom with which one sweeps the oven, even though this extinguishes [coals].

It is permitted to bake an oven full of bread even though one only needs one loaf—and this is specifically with their ovens, which were small and they would stick the bread to their walls, and because it is full there is no room for the heat to spread and the bread bakes well. But with our ovens, one should not bake more than what is needed.

It is permitted to seal the opening of the oven with clay and mud from the riverbank, provided that it was softened from the day before, or one makes a marking in it and detaches it to one side. But to knead clay on Yom Tov is forbidden. And it is permitted to knead ash to seal the opening of the oven.

**Things forbidden on Yom Tov for preparing roasted food. Containing 2 paragraph): **We do not heat stones to roast or bake upon them, because this hardens them. We do not break earthenware, and we do not cut paper to roast upon them. And we do not split a reed to make it like a spit for roasting.
One may crack nuts with a cloth, and we are not concerned that it might tear.

Several specific laws regarding the laws of Yom Tov, containing seven sections: A skewer that has been flattened, even though one could straighten it by hand, one may not fix it. Rema: This is specifically when one can roast with it without fixing it. But if one cannot roast with it as is, and it broke on Yom Tov itself, it is permitted to fix it (Tur). However, we do not instruct this to the public (Rabbi Yerucham, vol. 3), lest they come to fix it even when it broke before Yom Tov. And the same law applies to all utensils that are impossible to prepare before Yom Tov.

A skewer that one wishes to roast with, if it was longer than necessary—it is forbidden to cut it or to burn it. One may not sharpen a knife with its whetstone, but one may sharpen it upon wood, earthenware, or stone. This ruling is not taught to the public, lest they come to sharpen with a whetstone. When does this apply? When the knife can cut with difficulty or has become nicked. But if it cannot cut at all, one may not sharpen it even upon wood, lest one come to sharpen it with a whetstone.

Poultry that one fills with meat and eggs—it is permitted to sew them on Yom Tov, provided that he prepares the thread before Yom Tov and places it in the needle, and he should be careful not to cut the thread on Yom Tov. Rema: And so they customarily burn the thread that remains in the bird after they sewed with it.
It is permitted to cut on a Festival the bindings of young goats and fowl that are tied, and the threads that are sewn, and likewise one may burn a wick or rag with which the fowl is tied.

It is permitted on Yom Tov to heat an iron utensil in which cheese flatbreads were baked, and after the heating to bake in it a meat pastry, provided that when it is heated, it is placed on the food immediately. However, if it has absorbed [flavor] from non-kosher meat or the like, it is forbidden to heat it even to bake permitted food in it. Rema: Similarly, it is forbidden to purge vessels on Yom Tov (Mordechai end of Yoma, Or Zarua, and Hagahot Maimoniot chapter 1). And it is permitted to heat a spit on which unsalted meat was roasted when one wishes to roast with it again on Yom Tov (Maharai of Prague).
It is prohibited to make hole in a new barrel

To immerse a new utensil on Yom Tov, its law is the same as on Shabbat, as stated in section 223:7. Rema: And the law of rinsing and scrubbing utensils on Yom Tov — their laws are the same as on Shabbat, as stated in section 223. And it is permitted to move muktzeh (set-aside items) for the purpose of food preparation and the joy of Yom Tov.

**Various things forbidden on Yom Tov and which of them are permitted with a change. 11 sections:** One may rub ears of grain and crush legumes in the normal way on Yom Tov, and winnow a little at a time and eat — even using a basket or bowl, but not a board, sieve, or strainer.

One who sorts legumes on Yom Tov sorts in the normal way — in his lap or in a bowl (if he wishes to eat them that day) (HaMagid ch. 3) — but not on a board, sieve, or strainer. This applies when the edible portion is greater than the waste; but if the waste is greater than the edible portion, one removes the edible portion and leaves the waste. And if it would be more effort to remove the waste from the edible than to remove the edible from the waste, even if the edible is the greater portion, one removes the edible and leaves the waste. Rema: Almonds and pistachios that are cracked and still in their shells — the shell is not considered waste since that is their normal state and they are still mixed together. (Tur)
One may not strain mustard through its strainer, nor sweeten it with a wooden coal; but with a metal one it is permitted.

One may not hang a strainer on Yom Tov to filter sediment through it; but if it was already hanging, one may pour sediment into it to strain. One may use a ruse — hang it to put pomegranates in it, and then put sediment in it. Rema: The other laws of straining on Yom Tov are the same as on Shabbat, as stated in §319. (Beit Yosef)

One may not make cheese on Yom Tov. (And one may not curdle milk on Yom Tov.) (Hagahot Maimoniyot ch. 3, Ran end of ch. 4 of Beitzah, and Beit Yosef in the name of Rokeach) Similarly one may not make butter from milk on Yom Tov. (Rivash §121)
One may not cut vegetables with scissors that are normally used to cut them while still attached to the ground.

One may prepare cardoon and artichokes. Rema: It is permitted to salt many pieces of radish on Yom Tov if one wishes to eat them, even though it is forbidden on Shabbat — though some are stringent. (Maharil)

Even though carrying is permitted on Yom Tov even for non-essential purposes, one should not carry large loads in the same manner as on a weekday — one must make a change. How so? One who brings jugs of wine from place to place should not bring them in a basket or crate holding four or five jugs, but should bring them on his shoulder or in front of him, one or two at a time, which shows clearly that he is bringing them for Yom Tov needs. Rema: This applies specifically when carrying from place to place, but from corner to corner (Beit Yosef in the name of Rashi) or from house to house within the same courtyard (Or Zarua) it is permitted in any manner.
One who carries straw should not sling the basket behind his back but should carry it in his hand.

Similarly, loads that are normally carried on a pole should be carried on one's back; those normally carried on one's back should be carried on one's shoulder; those normally carried on the shoulder should be carried in front in one's hand, or a garment should be spread over them — and any similar change in how the load is carried. If it is impossible — such as when one has invited many guests and needs to hurry and bring things before them — one may do it in the normal way. This applies to carrying on a person, but on an animal one may not bring things at all.
One may not bring wood using a rope, basket, or mat, but may bring it in a cloth or in one's lap.

**Kindling a fire and heating water is permitted on Yom Tov. 4 sections:** It is permitted to make a bonfire to warm oneself by it. Rema: Some say it is forbidden to heat a winter room on Yom Tov, since sometimes the cold is not great and it is only for the pampered, making it like a bathhouse or fumigation which are forbidden. (Beit Yosef in the name of a German responsum, and the custom is to be lenient)

It is permitted to heat water on Yom Tov to wash one's hands, but not one's whole body — even if one does not wash it all at once. Rema: However, it is permitted to bathe a baby in water heated by a Jew on Yom Tov. (Mordechai ch. 3) But it is forbidden to heat water specifically for the baby's needs even through a non-Jew. (Mahara of Prague) However, when water is needed for cooking or rinsing, it is permitted to heat extra for the baby's sake. (Kol Bo) The law of the hot springs of Tiberias is the same as on Shabbat, as stated in §326. (Beit Yosef) But in water that was heated before Yom Tov it is permitted to wash one's whole body even all at once — however only outside a bathhouse, but in a bathhouse it is forbidden. Rema: Some forbid it in any case, and this is the custom. (Tur and Rosh)
A person is permitted to immerse on Yom Tov to purify himself from ritual impurity.

One may not make fumigation — meaning scattering spices over coals, whether to smell them or to fumigate a house or vessels. But if one does so in order to give a pleasant scent to fruits to improve them for eating, it is permitted even if one scatters them over a wood coal. Rema: It is forbidden to invert a perfumed cup over garments, since this creates a scent in them. (HaMagid ch. 1 and Hagahot Asheiri, end of ch. 2 of Beitzah)

**Not to cook for a non-Jew on Yom Tov. 3 sections:** One may not cook for a non-Jew on Yom Tov. Therefore it is forbidden to invite him, lest one cook extra on his account — and specifically inviting him Rema: to one's home; but sending food to his home via a non-Jew is permitted. (Hagahot Maimoniyot ch. 1 in the name of Or Zarua) But one's male or female servant, as well as a messenger who was sent to him, and similarly a non-Jew who comes on his own — it is permitted to feed them along with oneself, and we are not concerned that one will cook extra on their account. Rema: It is permitted to cook extra for one's male or female servant in the same pot one is cooking in for oneself. (Mordechai ch. 2 of Beitzah) But for other non-Jews it is forbidden in any case. (Orchot Chayyim and Tosafot) A Jew who bakes in a non-Jew's oven and must give him one loaf — he should not designate a specific loaf for the non-Jew before baking, as that would mean he is baking for the non-Jew; rather he should bake without designation and then give him one afterward. (Kol Bo)
Soldiers who gave their flour to a Jew to bake bread for them — if they do not object when the Jew gives some of it to a child, it is permitted to bake for them.

It is forbidden to cook or bake for dogs, but it is permitted to handle food and place it before them. Rema: But it is forbidden to carry it out for him from one domain to another. (Hagahot Maimoniyot and HaMagid ch. 1) Similarly it is forbidden to knead bran for fowl (Mordechai) except with a change. (Kol Bo) It is permitted to cook extra for the dogs in the same pot one is cooking in for oneself, even if one has something else one could give the dogs if one wished. (Beit Yosef in the name of Ran and the Yerushalmi)

**The law of an egg laid on Yom Tov. Containing 8 sections:** An egg laid on Yom Tov is forbidden to touch Rema: meaning to handle (Mordechai, beginning of Beitzah and ch. Kol HaKelim) and certainly not to eat. If it became mixed with others, even with a thousand, all are forbidden.
If there is doubt whether it was laid on Yom Tov or on a weekday, it is forbidden.

An egg laid on Yom Tov that was inadvertently cooked together with meat and a stew — if there is sixty times its volume in the mixture, everything is permitted except the egg itself. But if the stew was clarified by it or something similar — something that affects appearance and taste — it is not nullified.
It is permitted to invert a vessel over it so it does not break, provided the vessel does not touch it.

If it was laid on the first day of Yom Tov it is permitted on the second day of Yom Tov in the two days of Diaspora holidays. But for the two days of Rosh Hashanah, and similarly for Shabbat and Yom Tov that are adjacent to each other — if it was laid on one it is forbidden on the other. Rema: If Yom Tov falls on Sunday and Monday and the egg was laid on the preceding Shabbat, it is permitted on the second day of the Diaspora holiday. (Maharil)

An egg that emerged mostly before Yom Tov and then went back in and was afterward laid on Yom Tov — it is permitted. Therefore, even if one checked a hen's nest just before nightfall on the eve of Yom Tov and found no egg, and the next morning got up early and found an egg — it is permitted, since hens do not lay at night and we assume the greater part had already emerged the day before and went back in. This applies when there is a rooster within sixty houses with no river without a bridge separating them, for otherwise it is possible she laid at night and it would be forbidden. But if one did not check before Yom Tov, even if there is no rooster with her it is permitted, since we assume it was laid the day before — and without a rooster most hens lay during the day. Therefore it is permitted to buy eggs from a non-Jew on the first night of Yom Tov, as we assume they were laid on the eve of Yom Tov. Similarly on the second night of the two Diaspora Yom Tov days — but not on the second night of Rosh Hashanah, nor on the night of Yom Tov that follows Shabbat. Rema: A non-Jew who casually mentions that the eggs were laid yesterday may be relied upon. (Mordechai, beginning of Beitzah) This applies specifically to Yom Tov that falls in the middle of the week, but Yom Tov that falls on Sunday — where there is concern the egg was laid on Shabbat and is Biblically forbidden on Yom Tov — a non-Jew speaking casually is not believed. This applies only to the first day of Yom Tov, but on the second day, even Rosh Hashanah, he is believed since the prohibition is only Rabbinic. (Terumat HaDeshen §79)
One who slaughters a hen and finds fully formed eggs inside — they are permitted, even on Yom Tov that follows Shabbat.
A chick hatched on Yom Tov is forbidden. If it hatched on Shabbat it is forbidden on the Yom Tov that follows.

**Not to extinguish on Yom Tov. 11 sections:** It is forbidden to extinguish a fire on Yom Tov, even if one sees his house burning, as long as there is no danger to life. One may not extinguish a piece of wood even to prevent the house or pot from becoming smoky, or in order to have marital relations. Rema: Some say this applies only when it is possible to save the pot without extinguishing, but if it is impossible to save or cook the pot in any other way except by extinguishing, it is permitted to extinguish. [Rosh, Mordechai, Ran ch. 2 of Beitzah, Rashba, and Tur] This seems to me the primary ruling. Similarly regarding a house — if the house will burn and he will have no place to eat there and will lose his meal, it is permitted to extinguish; but if he has another house to eat in, it is forbidden to extinguish on account of financial loss. [Beit Yosef in the name of Orchot Chayyim]

Tilting a lamp to draw the oil away from the wick is considered extinguishing and is forbidden. Similarly it is forbidden to take a wick from a burning lamp even to place it in another lamp, since the moment one removes it one extinguishes it. Rema: It is permitted to add wicks to a burning lamp so that it burns strongly and goes out quickly. [Ran, ch. Ein Tzadin]

A wax candle that one wishes to light on Yom Tov, and one is concerned it will burn down entirely — one may place around it before lighting it something that prevents it from burning, so that it will go out when the flame reaches that point. Rema: Some permit cutting a wax candle with fire — meaning one lights it also from below in order to shorten it — and this is the custom. But cutting it with a knife is forbidden. [Hagahot Maimoniyot ch. 6, Hagahot Asheiri, Mordechai, and Tosafot ch. 1 of Beitzah] It is permitted to place a lamp in a spot where the wind blows in order for it to go out, but it is forbidden to place it there if the wind is already blowing. [Maharil]

A lamp that went out and one wishes to relight it that same day — one may trim the top of the wick so that it will be easy to light. Rema: Leftover oil and wicks are permitted even on Yom Tov that follows Shabbat, or the two days of Rosh Hashanah. (Beit Yosef in the name of most authorities)

A lamp lit for no purpose — meaning one does not need it — it is forbidden to light. But a synagogue lamp is not considered purposeless and it is permitted to light it even on the second day of Yom Tov after Mincha, and there is no concern of preparing for a weekday, since in lighting it there is a mitzvah for that moment. To fix the wicks and the lamps on Yom Tov after Mincha — if one wishes to light them that same day it is permitted; if not, it is forbidden.
One may not place a lamp on a tree from before Yom Tov, since we are concerned one may come to make use of the tree.
One may not open a clay lamp — meaning while it is still soft like a potter's clay vessel — by pressing it with one's hand to make a hollow in it, since one would be making a vessel.
One may not cut a wick in two, unless one inserts both its ends into two lamps and lights it in the middle, and only when one needs both lamps.

One may not braid a wick nor singe it; but if it is not hard enough one may press it with one's hand to harden it, and it is permitted to soak it in oil [in which there is no burning lamp]. [Beit Yosef in the name of the Rokeach]
It is permitted to remove the charred tip from the top of a burning lamp, but one may not cut the top of the wick with a utensil.
One who lights a Yom Tov lamp must recite the blessing: Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who has commanded us to light the Yom Tov lamp.

**Laws of items brought on Yom Tov from outside the Shabbat boundary. Containing 9 paragraphs:** If a non-Jew brought a gift to a Jew on Yom Tov, if there is produce of that type still attached to the ground, or if it requires trapping, it is forbidden even to someone for whom it was not brought, to eat it that same day. [And even if one transgressed and put it in his mouth and chewed it, he may not swallow it.] [R. Shimshon in his commentary to Mishnah, Terumot ch. 2] Even to handle it is forbidden. After the holiday it is permitted after waiting the time it would have taken to perform the action. For the two days of Yom Tov observed in the Diaspora, if it was brought on the first day it is permitted immediately on the night of the second Yom Tov after waiting that time. Rema: Some are stringent and forbid it until after the second Yom Tov ends [Tur in the name of Rabbeinu Tam, Rashi, and Semag], and the custom is to be stringent if it is not needed for Yom Tov itself — but for guests and similar circumstances the custom is to be lenient for others for whom it was not brought [Terumat HaDeshen §78]. Similarly, if it was brought on the second Yom Tov, one must wait after Yom Tov ends for the required time. But for the two days of Rosh Hashanah, or for Yom Tov adjacent to Shabbat whether before or after — if it was brought on the first day one must wait until after both Yom Tov and Shabbat end, plus the required time. The measure of "time it would have taken" means the time for the non-Jew to go to the place where he gathered it, complete the work, and return. If it is uncertain from where he brought it, the measure is the time it would take to come from outside the boundary.

Even if the non-Jew detached or trapped the items for himself, or they fell from the tree on their own, or were caught on their own — it is forbidden to eat them that day or to handle them, even for someone for whom they were not brought. But after the holiday they are permitted immediately at the close of Yom Tov, even for the one for whom they were brought.

Even if there is doubt whether they were gathered or trapped that day, they are forbidden. But if it is evident that they were not gathered or trapped that day, it is permitted for one for whom they were not brought. And if they did not come from outside the boundary, it is permitted even for the one for whom they were brought. Rema: A non-Jew who speaks casually that it was not gathered or trapped today is believed. [See above Siman 413, section 6.]

If a non-Jew brought a gift to a Jew consisting of items whose species is still attached to the ground — on the first day of Rosh Hashanah that falls on Thursday — some permit eating them on Shabbat after waiting the required time, and some forbid it. Rema: According to our custom to be stringent regarding the two Yom Tov days of the Diaspora, the same rule applies there. Regarding the halachic ruling: it seems that for the two days of Rosh Hashanah one should be stringent regarding Shabbat, but for the two Yom Tov days of the Diaspora one may be lenient regarding a Shabbat that follows them — and specifically for fruits that do not require preparation on the Yom Tov preceding Shabbat; but something that needs to be prepared on the second Yom Tov for Shabbat is forbidden, since the custom is to forbid it — and even to handle it on the second Yom Tov, unless it is for guests or similar needs. (Terumat HaDeshen §78)

Something whose species is not attached to the ground and does not require trapping — if it came from within the boundary it is permitted to everyone. If it came from outside the boundary, it is forbidden to eat for the one for whom it was brought and all members of his household, but it is permitted to handle it within four cubits, or within a walled city, or a fortified settlement known to have been enclosed for dwelling purposes. Others are permitted even to eat it. After the holiday [the first Yom Tov], the one for whom it was brought must wait the required time. Rema: After that time it is permitted even according to our custom of being stringent in other matters, as explained above.

In a city where the majority of residents are non-Jews, it is assumed that whoever brings produce brings it for the majority. Rema: If it is half and half, or it is known that he gathered it for both Jews and non-Jews, it is forbidden. [Beit Yosef and Semag]

If it is uncertain whether the items came from outside the boundary — if the non-Jew lives with him in the city and such fruits are commonly found in the city, it is permitted; otherwise it is forbidden.

Something whose species is not attached to the ground that was brought to a Jew on the first day of Rosh Hashanah is permitted on the second day. The same applies to Shabbat and Yom Tov that are adjacent to each other.

If a Jew sent a gift to his fellow via a non-Jew from before Yom Tov, and the non-Jew was delayed and brought it on Yom Tov from outside the boundary — it is permitted even to the one for whom it was brought to eat it. However, it is forbidden for any Jew to handle it beyond four cubits, or outside a walled city, or outside a fortified settlement known to have been enclosed for dwelling purposes. Rema: This applies specifically when the sender had it in mind the day before, so there is no prohibition of muktzeh. But if he did not have it in mind the day before, even though there is no violation of the boundary laws, it is still forbidden due to muktzeh, since anything belonging to a Jew requires designation before the holiday — and even for one for whom it was not brought it is forbidden. [Beit Yosef in the name of a responsum of the Rashba]

Since carrying was permitted for the sake of food preparation, it was also permitted for the sake of non-(food preparation), such as (for the sake of) a minor, a Lulav, a Sefer Torah, and vessels. Rema: (Provided) that one needs them a bit, or if one is afraid lest they be stolen or suffer some other loss (Hagahot Semak & R. Yerucham) but (carrying) stones and the like is prohibited. Rema: And it is permitted to play with a ball, even in the public domain, despite the fact that it is mere recreation (Tosafot & R. Yerucham). And if one established a "eruv" it is permitted to handle and carry anything that is considered a vessel, even though it has no need that day at all (Ran, Beitzah Chapter 2).
Sweeping the House, One Siman: The law of sweeping the house is the same on a holiday as it is on Shabbat (and see above chapter 337).

The Law The Law of Moving Fruits from Place to Place on a Holiday, and it has 3 Simanim: 1. We can drop fruits through a trapdoor (meaning, from "when your olives will drop" (Deuteronomy 28:40), as in, when fruits fall to the ground) on a holiday. One should not drop them through windows nor lower them on a ladder nor carry them from roof to roof, even if the two are the same (height).
2. It is permitted to cover fruit, wine jugs, or bricks because of water leaking [through the roof].
3. Regarding putting a dish under dripping water, the rule on a holiday is the same as the rule on Shabbat (and see above chapter 338 paragraph 8).

**A few things that are forbidden to be carried on Yom Tov, and there are 4 Simanim: ** The blind man may not leave with his stick nor the shepherd with his sack (and the law of a disabled person is the same on a holiday as it is on Shabbat, see above chapter 301 paragraph 17).
Neither a man nor a woman may go out in a [carried] chair. If many people need him, it is permitted, and he may be carried on the shoulders, even in a litter (or a canopy).
Someone whose legs have shrunk (meaning that they have become shorter) can leave with his stick.
We do not lead an animal with a stick.
1. Laws regarding animals on the holiday, 4 Seifim: We remove flies that are stuck on an animal, even though this creates a wound.
2. We do not comb an animal with a fine comb on a holiday because this removes hair.
3. We do not deliver an animal on a holiday, but we assist it by holding the newborn such that it does not fall on the ground, blowing in its nose, and putting the teat into its mouth.

4. If an animal spurns its newborn, it is permitted to sprinkle (meaning to pour) the water of the after-birth on it and put salt in her womb so that she will have mercy on it. It is forbidden to do this for an impure animal. Rem"a: (And see above chapter 246 paragraph 3 in the Rem"a's note regarding whether a man is commanded to let his animal rest on a holiday).

1. Some things that are forbidden on a holiday, 2 Seifim: We do not climb a tree, ride on an animal, swim in water, slap the hand on the thigh, clap hands, dance, make legal judgments, get engaged, get married, divorce, perform a Levirate marriage, do halitzah, make a cherem vow, or separate trumah or tithes. Rem"a: Regarding redeeming the first born, the rule on a holiday is the same as the rule on Shabbat. See above in chapter 339 paragraph 4.
2. One who is dangerously ill and will leave the world soon is permitted to divorce, even on Shabbat.
1. The Law of Lending on a holiday, 2 Seifim: A loan made on a holiday can be claimed (and see above chapter 307 paragraph 11).

2. The charity collectors may collect from the yards on a holiday, but they should not make announcements as are made during the week. Rather, they should collect quietly, put it in their bag, and distribute it to each neighborhood individually.

1. The laws of death on a holiday, 12 Seifim: If a dead body is waiting to be buried on the first day of a holiday (a Jew should not busy himself with it, even if it will smell and it is possible to use non-Jews, but) non-Jews can busy themselves with it, even if he died that day (and see above chapter 304), and even if they can wait until the next day when it will smell. This is all referring to making the (grave), the coffin, and the shrouds. However, dressing him, heating water to purify him, and taking it out to put it in the grave is permitted even for a Jew. Rem"a: And it is best to be careful to purify him over a straw, leather, or wood, and not over sheets, lest one come to [transgress the prohibition of] wringing (Trumat Hadeshen chapter 82).
If somebody dies on the first day of a holiday, it is forbidden to let him rest until the second day so that Jews can deal with him.
3. On Shabbat and Yom Kippur, not even non-Jews can deal with him, even by carrying him out by handing and putting him in a kuf (meaning, a plot) that was made the previous day.

On the second day of a holiday, even Rosh Hashana, Jews may deal with the corpse, even if it has not been sitting around. They may even cut myrtle from the ground, make him shrouds and a coffin, dig out a plot, heat water for purification, or cut his hair. If the city has no Jewish cemetery, we take him to another city that has Jewish plots, even outside of the techum. We rent a boat to take him from place to place. This is all because the second day of a holiday is Rabbinically equal to a weekday when it comes to death. Even if non-Jews can deal with him, Jews do. Rem"a: In Ashkenaz and these countries, we do not do this. Rather, inasmuch as non-Jews can make the grave, coffin, and shrouds, we have them do this. Everything else is done by Jews, as on the first day of the holiday. However, if it is not possible to have non-Jews do it, Jews are allowed to do everything (Mordechai, Laws of Mourning and Trumat Hadeshen chapter 82). [The list of allowed labors] does not include the dome that is made over the grave, which we do not build on a holiday. Rem"a: However, it is permitted to cover him with dirt as is done on a weekday (Beit Yosef), and we do not follow those who are stringent in this matter. This is restricted to cases where we want to bury him that day. However, if we do not want to bury him that day, we do not perform any prohibited labor for him, even using a non-Jew, but carrying is permitted. (the laws of saying the Shma and praying when one's immediate relative has died on the first or second day of a holiday can be found above in chapter 71 paragraph 2 and below in chapter 548 paragraph 5]].)
One who digs a grave on the second day of a holiday is permitted to receive payment.

6. It is permitted to accompany a corpse on the first day of a holiday within the techum. On the second day of the holiday, it is allowed even outside of the techum. We then return that day. It is also permitted to bring back the digging tools that were brought outside of the techum.

7. Those who accompany the dead are forbidden to ride on an animal, even on the second day of a holiday. this applies even to the mourners and the ones who bury. If this is impossible, we permit them to ride on an animal on the second day of a holiday.

8. If the residents of one city find out that a Jew died four or five days away and cannot be buried, they are permitted to set out on the second day of the holiday to bury him quickly, even if they will not get there until after the holiday. Rem"a: It is permitted to bring a dead person on the second day of a holiday from outside of the techum to the city in order to bury him in a Jewish cemetery, even if it is possible to bury him where he is (Beit Yosef in the name of the responsa of the Rashb"a).

9. If an infant died in its first thirty days and it had grown hair and nails, it is considered a child that will endure. It is treated like an dead adult, even if we do not know if it was brought fully to term, because most women give birth to children that will endure.

10. Those who have the practice to remove fetuses' foreskin with a rock or reed are prohibited from doing so even on the second day of a holiday. Rem"a: It is prohibited to bury it that day. Rather, we wait until tomorrow (Beit Yosef).
We do not tear for the dead, even on the second day of a holiday. This applies even to immediate relatives.

12. When somebody dies on the second night of a holiday, we wake up early and bury him before prayers. When somebody dies during the day, we bury him after eating. Rem"a: The laws of Tziduk Hadin on a holiday are found in Yoreah Deah chapter 401 paragraph 6.

1. The Laws of Eruv Tavshilin, 24 Seifim: If a holiday falls on Friday, one should not cook something for Shabbat in its own pot. One can cook many pots for the holiday and if he makes too much, the leftovers are for Shabbat. Using an eruv, one can cook for Shabbat. (Meaning that the point of the eruv is so that one can cook and bake on a holiday for Shabbat along with what was already baked or cooked for Shabbat before the holiday, so that he is not starting the work on the holiday but is just finishing it.) Rem"a: It is permitted to make the eruv even at twilight (Mordechai at the end of Chapter "Bameh Madlikin").
2. This eruv consists of bread and a cooked item. If one only made it using a cooked item, it is permitted.

3. The measure of this cooked item must be a kezayit (olive's weight), whether [the eruv] is for one person or for a thousand, at all points of its existence. Rem"a: Some require the bread to be a kebeitzah (egg's weight) (Yerushalmi) and such is the practice, initially.
4. The cooked item must be something that accompanies bread - not barley.

5. The cooked item can be roasted, stewed, pickled or smoked. It can even be the small fish that are prepared by putting them in hot water and this is how they are cooked - one can rely on them. It can be cooked apples (the same goes for other cooked fruits) or small fish that were boiled.
One can rely upon lentils that are at the bottom of the pot before the holiday, or fat stuck to the knife that is scraped off, as long as it is a kezayit (olive's worth).

7. It is a mitzvah for everyone to make an eruv. It is incumbent on the leader of the city to make an eruv for his townspeople so that those who forgot to make an eruv, those who were forced not to, and those who made an eruv and lost it can rely on his. (This is also the case for ignoramuses who do not know who to make an eruv) (Or Zarua). However, one who can make an eruv and didn't make an eruv but rather wanted to depend on the leader's eruv is called a sinner and cannot rely on it.

8. When one makes an eruv for others, he need not specify (that). Rather, he can make it generally for all the residents of the town, and all who live within the techum (boundaries) of the town can rely on it. Rem"a: However, somebody outside of the techum cannot rely on it, even if he made an eruv techumin and can enter [the town], unless the maker of the eruv mentioned him explicitly (the Magid chapter 6).

9. The maker of the eruv must intend to exempt others, but he who is the beneficiary of the eruv does not need to intend such when the eruv is made. He [the eruv maker] should tell him on the holiday before starting to cook for Shabbat. Rem"a: If the leader generally makes an eruv for everybody, we rely on it by default (Ra"n chapter 2).

10. One who makes an eruv for others must transfer possession to them using a [symbolic] person. And everybody who can be used for a Shabbat eruv can be used for an eruv tavshilin, and everybody who cannot be used for that eruv cannot be used for this eruv. (And see above chapter 366).
11. The one who receives the eruv must lift it off of the ground a tefach (a handsbreath).

[The maker of the eruv] then takes the eruv from he who received it and blesses "...on the commandment of eruv." He then says "With this it will be permitted to bake, cook, insulate, light lamps, and do all that is needed for Shabbat on the holiday, for us and for X and for Y" or "for all the residents of this city." Rem"a: And one who doesn't know the holy language can say it in the vernacular that he understands (the Mahari"l).
Even with an eruv, one cannot cook on the first day of the holiday for Shabbat.

14. If one made the eruv with the intention of relying on it as long as it exists, even on a different holiday, he should initially not rely on it on a different holiday, but after the fact, he can rely on it.
15. If the eruv was eaten or lost before one cooked for Shabbat, he cannot cook unless a kezayit (olive's weight) remains.
16. After preparing for Shabbat, he can eat it.
17. If one started making dough and then the eruv was eaten, he can finish that dough. It is also the case that if one started to cook, he can finish the dish he started.

If one baked but did not cook or cooked but did not bake and then the eruv was eaten or lost, what he legally made, even if it was intended for the holiday, can be left for Shabbat. He can then cook more food for the holiday.
19. One who didn't make an eruv is allowed to light the Shabbat candle. There are some who forbid this.

20. If one did not make an eruv, just as it is forbidden for him to cook for himself, it is also forbidden for him to cook for others, even in their houses. Others are also forbidden to cook for him. The only solution is for him to give his flour and cooked things as a gift to others with an eruv. They can then bake and cook and give it to him. They can even cook in his house. If there are no others with an eruv, some say that he is permitted to minimally bake one loaf, cook one dish, and light one candle. Rem"a: If he made an eruv but did not specify the labors explicitly, just saying "With this it will be permitted for us to do all needed things," he is like somebody who made no eruv (Or Zarua). Somebody fasting on a holiday is forbidden to cook for others even for that day, because he is likened to somebody who made no eruv and is forbidden to cook for others (Maharil).

21. If one realized that he did not make an eruv before the morning meal, he can cook a lot in one pot and the leftovers will be for Shabbat. Rem"a: He can also go during the day into a room with a lit candle to look for something and leave it lit until night (Tur). There are some who permit even cooking in many pots, because it is before eating. This only holds when one eats from each one [that day].

22. If one realized that he didn't make an eruv on the first day of the holiday and it is Rosh Hashana, he cannot make an eruv on condition. However, if it is a Diasporean holiday, he can make an eruv on a condition: If today is holy, I do not need an eruv, and if today is a weekday, with this eruv it will be permitted for us to bake and cook... The next day, he need not say anything. Some say that if he doesn't have anything that was cooked yesterday, his condition does not work.
23. If one sinned intentionally (or unintentionally) and cooked many dishes not for the sake of the holiday, he can eat them on Shabbat or a weekday.
24. If one tried to circumvent the law by cooking two dishes for today and leaving one leftover for tomorrow, he is forbidden to eat it.

The Laws of Eruvei Chatzeirot (courtyard eruvin). Containing 2 paragraphs: On a holiday, making eruvs for yards and conjoining alleys are unnecessary, but techum eruvs are necessary. All of the laws of techum were explained in the section on laws for techum eruvs.

If a holiday falls on Friday, we do not make either yard or techum eruvs (even if one made an eruv tavshilin) (Ra"n chapter 2 of Beitzah) . However, if one realized on the first day of a two day holiday in the Diaspora [that he didn't make an eruv], he can make an yard eruv on condition [see previous chapter paragraph 22]. However, we do not make techum eruvs on a holiday (under any circumstances).

**The Laws of Being Joyful on a Yom Tov. Containing 4 paragraphs:** It is a holiday mitzvah to spend half the time in the House of Study and half of the time eating and drinking. One should not skimp on holiday expenses; it must be honored and enjoyed like Shabbat. Rema: It is forbidden to eat after Mincha on the day before a holiday, just like for Shabbat, and this is part of honoring it (Rambam chapter 6). However, if the day before the holiday is Shabbat, one can have the third meal and eat a bit of bread in honor of the holiday. It is a mitzvah to knead bread on the day before the holiday in honor of the holiday (Mahari"l laws of a holiday) like on Friday, as was explained above in chapter 342. It is an obligation to eat two loaves of bread and to include wine in the meal. Holiday clothes should be nicer than those for Shabbat. It is not the practice to make a third meal. And on a holiday, we tarry when going to synagogue and quickly leave synagogue because of the holiday joy (Gemara end of chapter "Hakoreh Omed").

2. It is an obligation for a man to be happy and in good spirits on the holiday - him, his wife, his kids, and all who are with him. How should he make them happy? He should give the children nuts and the women new clothes and jewelry according to his finances. One is obligated to feed the stranger, the orphan, and the widow, along with other poor people. (The rules of fasting on a holiday are the same as for Shabbat, and see above chapter 388.)

3. One should eat, drink, and be happy on the holiday. One should not overindulge in meat, wine, laughter, or frivolity, because laughter and frivolity are not happiness but debauchery and foolishness. We were not commanded to engage in debauchery and frivolity but only happiness that involves worshipping the Creator.

4. The court must appoint officers who will walk around patrolling gardens, orchards, and rivers, so that men and women will not gather there to eat and drink and end up sinning. They should similarly warn the whole nation about this - that men and women should not joyously mix in houses and overindulge in wine, lest they come to sin. Rather, all should be holy.
1. On Chol Hamoed, some labors are prohibited and some are permitted. Rem"a: According to the need, the Sages saw fit to permit.
1. The Laws of Shaving on Chol Hamoed, 8 Seifim: It is a mitzvah to shave on the day before a holiday.
2. One may not shave during the holiday, even if he shaved before the holiday.
3. Even if one was forced and thus did not shave on the day before the holiday, he should not shave during hol hamoed. This is also the rule for one who was sick and got better during the holiday.

4. The following people may shave during the holiday: he who left captivity and did not have an opportunity to shave before the holiday; he who left jail, even if he was imprisoned by Jews who would have allowed him to shave; he who was banned [formally by the community] and allowed [back into the community] during the holiday; he who vowed not to shave and asked for the nullification of his vow during the holiday; he who arrived from abroad during hol hamoed or who arrived on the day before the holiday but didn't have time that day to shave, assuming that he did not go from Israel to outside of Israel for recreational purposes.
5. Even in instances where it is permitted to get a haircut, one should not get a haircut in the public domain. Rather, one should do this in private.
6. A child can be shaved during the holiday, even if he was born before the holiday (and this is even allowed in public) (this follows from the Mordechai).

7. If a mourner's seventh day [of mourning] falls on a Shabbat that is the day before a holiday, he is permitted to shave on hol hamoed. Rem"a: He who left Judaism, returned, and normally shaves is permitted to shave on hol hamoed (Trumat Hadeshen chapter 86).

8. Every man is permitted to remove his mustache on hol hamoed. Rem"a: Even in public. It is permitted to rub the head and to comb even though this will remove hair - it is not considered shaving (Mordechai at the beginning of Moed Katan).

**Cutting Nails on Chol HaMoed. Containing 2 paragraphs:** It is permitted to cut fingernails and toenails, even with scissors. Rema: But there are some who are stringent and forbid this. The practice is to be stringent not to cut them, whether with a knife or scissors, if it is not for the mitzvah of immersion, when they should be cut as they are normally done on a weekday (Sma"k and Tosafot).
Everything medical is allowed on hol hamoed.

**Work that is Permitted on Chol HaMoed. Containing 5 paragraphs: ** It is permitted to grind flour for a holiday need, even if one planned to do thi on the holiday. [The same is true for] cutting trees from the ground or making mead, whether it is from dates or barley, for a holiday need. If it is not for a holiday need, it is forbidden. However, one need not minimize production - rather, one can make a lot, and if he makes too much, he makes too much. However, one should not circumvent the law by grinding too much or making too much (mead) intentionally. Alternatively, if one has flour (or old mead) he should not circumvent the law (to make more) and say, "I want from this [new] batch." However, if one has bread, he is permitted to grind [wheat] (for bread), because warm bread is preferrable. This is also the law for mead - if the new is actually better than the old, it is allowed (the Magid chapter 7).

It is permitted to uproot flax because it can be used to cover foods, to uproot hops because it can be used to make mead needed on the holiday, and to uproot sesame because the dry ones can be eaten immediately.

If fruits have ripened a bit such that they can be eaten in a stretch, it is permitted to collect them in order to eat them. If one collected them to eat them, collected too much, and he now worries that they will rot if they are not pickled to remove the moisture, he can pickle them. However, it is forbidden to collect in order to pickle. If there is something that won't be available after the holiday, it is permitted to buy it and pickle it.

A man can catch as many fish as he can catch and then salt all of them on the holiday. This is because it is possible to eat them on the holiday by squeezing them by hand many times until they are soft. (It is permitted to catch [fish] in public, because it is clear that it is for the holiday) (Mordechai).

For any labor that is done for a holiday need, if one also does it professionally, it must be done in private. How so? Hunters (of animals and birds), grinders, and those who pick grapes to sell in the market should do it in private when done for a holiday need. Rema: It is permitted to milk an animal even not to fulfill a holiday need, because it will result in loss otherwise (Trumat Hadeshen chapter 153 and Beit Yosef).

1. The Laws of Laundry on Chol Hamoed, 3 Seifim: We do not do laundry on hol hamoed. The following may do laundry: someone who came from abroad, someone who left captivity or jail, one who was [formally] banned [by the community] and allowed [back into the community] by the elders during the holiday, one who swore not to do laundry and asked for the nullification of his vow during the holiday and received allowance. [We may also launder] hand rags, haircut rags, towels, and children's clothes. [The following may also launder:] a woman who found a stain [of menstruation] during the holiday and someone who only has one outfit. All of these can launder normally, even using carbonates or ahal (meaning types of soap) or in public at the river. Rem"a: However, they should only launder clothes that they need - one outfit (Mordechai and Hagahot Ashri chapter "Elu Megalchin"). However, infant's clothing, meaning those that we wrap them in in which they urinate and defecate, can be washed four or five at once, because many are needed at any given moment. Where it says above that it is permitted to launder in public, this is restricted to when one launders by the river because laundry is better by the river. However, when one does not launder by the river, he should launder in private and not in public. This seems right to me.
2. Any flax garment can be laundered. This is not our practice, and this is one of things that are permitted and others acted stringently where one is now not allowed to allow it for them.

3. We bring home things that are for the holiday from the artisan's place, like cushions, chairs, and saucers. However, objects that are not for the holiday like plows and wool from the painter should not be brought. If the artisan has nothing to eat, one should pay him and leave [the goods] there. If he does not trust [the artisan], he can leave them in an adjacent house. If he is scared they will be stolen, he can move them to a different yard. However, he should only bring them home covertly.

**One Should not Move Things From Yard to Yard on Chol Hamoed, 3 Seifim:** One may not remove his things from yard to yard, even from a bad one to a nice one. One may not remove his things from his dwelling or move things that are not being moved for a holiday need. Rema: How much more so is it prohibited to move one's money from city to city (Mordechai chapter "Mi sheHafach"). However, one can remove things from house to house within one yard. If the houses open to an alley and not to a yard, there are some who say that he may move things between adjacent houses. Rema: If he fears for theft in the yard in which he lives, he can move even from his yard to a protected yard. Even moving things from city to city is permitted when there is potential loss (Hagahot Ashri and Mordechai).
There are some who permit him to move from another's yard to his yard, even from a nice yard to a bad one.
It is forbidden to remove manure in the yard. Rather, it should be moved to the sides. If there is so much of it that the yard has become like a stable, it can be removed to the dunghill.

**All Animal Needs Can Be Done on Chol Hamoed, 4 Seifim:** One who needs to ride on an animal to travel for pleasure or for a holliday need and cannot walk is permitted to trim the horse's hoofs, to fix its horseshoes, saddle, and bridle, and to do any other activity necessary for riding. This assumes that one did not plan to do this work on the holiday. Rema: It is permitted to ride on Chol Hamoed even from city to city and even for no reason, and this is the practice. However, it is prohibited to do activities necessary for riding if one rides neither for a holiday need nor for travel for pleasure (Beit Yosef).
It is permitted to brush a horse to make it prettier.
We do not breed animals on the holiday, but we do draw blood. We do not withhold anything medical, even if it involves labor.

We do not sit a hen on eggs to grow chicks. If she was placed before the holiday and ran away, one can return her (but it is forbidden to put a different one there, even if the first one died) (Beit Yosef). This is only the case when it is within three days of her running away.

1. The Law of Labor When There is Potential Loss, 16 Seifim: [Work where there is] a potential loss is permitted on hol hamoed with no change in how it is done. (However, any way to minimize the labor should be done) (Kol Bo). Therefore, a house of channels (meaning land that requires water) that was watered before the holiday can be watered [on hol hamoed]. Because one started to water it beforehand, if he does not water it now, it will be lost. However, it is forbidden to water a baal-plot - one that is watered only to make it nicer.

2. Even a house of channels is only allowed to be watered when there is not excessive labor involved, like when there is a spring, whether newly-emerged or old, that one can just extend and water the field. However, one should not draw water and irrigate from a pool or from gathered rainwater, because it involves much labor. Even if there is one garden bed, half high and half low, we do not draw water from the low one to water the high one.

3. One may water a house of channels on hol hamoed from a river that flows from a lake, assuming it has not stopped flowing. One can similarly water from channels that flow between pools. If a pool gets tricklings from a house of channels and it still trickles, one can water a different house of channels from it, assuming that the spring irrigating the upper house of channels has not stopped.

4. If one wants to eat vegetables on a holiday, he can draw water to irrigate them so that they will grow and be fit [for eating] on the holiday. If he does not want to eat them on the holiday and does such to make them nicer, it is forbidden.

5. We do not make pits at the roots of vines so that they will fill with water. If they were made and broke, one can fix them on hol hamoed (but it is forbidden to make them deeper than before) (the Magid chapter 8).
6. If a channel has broken, one may repair it. If it was one tefach deep, he can dig it out to six [tefachim]. If it was two tefachim deep, he can dig it out to seven.
7. Water can be drawn from tree to tree as long as the whole field is not watered thereby. If the field is moist, it is permitted to water all of it.

8. It is forbiden to open something up so that water can flow into a field and irrigate it. If one does this to gather fish to eat them on the holiday, like by opening something above for the water [and fish] to enter and below something to let [the water out], it is permitted.
9. It is forbidden to level off the field for plowing. If it is apparent that the intention is to thresh for holiday purposes, like if he levels all of it, it is permitted.

10. It is forbidden to gather wood from the field in order to make it better for plowing. If it is obvious that the intent is because he needs wood, like if he takes the big pieces and leaves the small, it is permitted.

11. It is forbidden to trim branches of a tree to fix [the tree]. If it is obvious that he does it for the branches in order to feed them to his animals and not to fix [the tree], like if he cuts only from one side, it is permitted.
12. We do not remove worms from a tree, nor do we patch (meaning stick dung there so that the tree will not die) saplings. However, we do smear oil on trees and fruits.

13. Moles and mice in an orchard can be trapped the normal way - by digging a hole and hanging a trip in there. It is even permitted to normally trap [rodents] in a vegetable field that is adjacent to an orchard, because they leave the field and destroy trees. If it is not adjacent to an orchard, we do not trap there using the normal procedure: one should stick a pole in the ground and shake it to and fro until a hole is made in which the trap can be hung. There are some who say that in a vegetable field adjacent to an orchard, the normal way is not allowed, and if it is not adjacent to an orchard, it is forbidden even with a change.

14. We do not bring cattle on Chol Hamoed to fertilize the field. If a non-Jew brought them by himself, this is allowed even on Shabbat, and even if bringing them in is seen as a favor, as long as no payment as given. It is even forbidden to give food as payment. On a holiday, it is permitted to give food as payment, as long as no other payment is given. On hol hamoed, even other payment is allowed, as long as he is not hired, aided, or given a watchman to direct the cattle (meaning to move them around and thereby direct the excrement). If the non-Jew is employed by the week, month, or year, he can be aided on hol hamoed and given a watchman to direct the cattle.

15. It is forbidden to harvest a field on Chol Hamoed if no loss will be incurred by letting it wait until after the holiday. If he has nothing to eat, even if there is what to buy in the market, we do not require him to buy from the market. Rather, he can reap, gather, thresh, winnow, and sort as usual, as long as he does not thresh with cows. This is only true when only he alone needs. However, if he must thresh for the masses, he can thresh even with cows.

16. If one has a vineyard adjacent to a non-Jew's vineyard, the non-Jew harvests his on hol hamoed, and if the Jew also does not harvest his, he will incur loss, he is permitted to harvest it, trample the grapes, make the barrels, and do all the activities for making wine with no change. This is only true when one did not plan to do this work on Chol Hamoed.
